summary: Provides encapsulation formats and semantics for emulating SONET/SDH circuits and services over MPLS, letting traditional telephone-style optical circuits travel across a packet network.

plainLanguage.summary: SONET and SDH carry telephone and data traffic on fixed-rate optical circuits. This RFC describes how to carry such a circuit across a packet network instead. The circuit is cut into pieces, each piece is wrapped in a small header, and the pieces are sent as ordinary packets. The far end puts the pieces back together at the original fixed rate.

subtitle: How a SONET or SDH optical circuit is carried across a packet network as a stream of framed packets.

tldr.problem: Telecommunications operators run optical circuits built on SONET and SDH, but the transport network is migrating to IP and MPLS. The circuits have to keep working across a packet network that delivers variable-size packets with variable delay.
tldr.mechanism: The Synchronous Payload Envelope or Virtual Tributary is cut into fragments, and each fragment is given a CEP header with a sequence number and a structure pointer, optionally an RTP header, then sent as an MPLS pseudowire. The receiving end reassembles the fragments at a fixed rate and plays them back onto the SONET or SDH interface.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4842 is a Proposed Standard from April 2007 that defines the encapsulation and semantics for emulating SONET and SDH circuits over MPLS packet-switched networks. It also defines optional ways to save bandwidth and the signaling parameters a pseudowire needs.

facts.label: Packet size that MUST be supported

today: RFC 4842 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 5143, an earlier version of the same work.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4842 provides encapsulation formats and semantics for emulating Synchronous Optical Network (SONET) and Synchronous Digital Hierarchy (SDH) circuits and services over MPLS packet-switched networks. The generic requirements and architecture for Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) are in RFC 3916 and RFC 3985, and additional requirements for emulating SONET/SDH and lower-rate time-division-multiplexed circuits are in RFC 4197.

The document defines emulation of two families of signal. The first is the Synchronous Payload Envelope (SPE) or Virtual Container: STS-1/VC-3, STS-3c/VC-4, STS-12c/VC-4-4c, STS-48c/VC-4-16c, STS-192c/VC-4-64c and similar. The second is the smaller Virtual Tributary (VT) or Virtual Container: VT1.5/VC-11, VT2/VC-12, VT3 and VT6/VC-2. Throughout the document these are called SONET/SDH channels.

The basic idea is simple. To carry a SONET/SDH circuit through a packet-oriented network, the SPE or VT is broken into fragments, and a CEP header and optionally an RTP header are prepended to each fragment. A pseudowire is the resulting connection across the packet network.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC covers two sizes of signal: the large Synchronous Payload Envelope used for high-rate circuits, and the smaller Virtual Tributary used for low-rate ones. In both cases the work is the same: cut the signal into fragments, put a header on each fragment, and send the fragments as packets.

sections.title: The CEP Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
The basic CEP packet has three parts: the PSN and multiplexing layer headers, the CEP header, and an optional RTP header, followed by the SONET/SDH fragment itself. The CEP header supports a basic mode, which gives the minimum needed to emulate a circuit accurately, and an extended mode used by some of the optional fragment formats.

The CEP header carries a set of small fields. The L bit signals CEP-AIS to the downstream provider edge, meaning a failure was detected on the attachment circuit. The R bit signals CEP-RDI upstream, meaning the sender has lost packet synchronization; it MUST be set to 0 once synchronization is acquired. The N and P bits explicitly relay negative and positive pointer adjustments across the packet network, and their use is optional; if unused they MUST be 0. The FRG bits MUST be set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

The Length field, when not zero, gives the length of the CEP header plus the RTP header if used plus the payload. It MUST be set when that total is 64 bytes or less and MUST be set to 0 otherwise, and when the payload is suppressed the Length field MUST be set to the header lengths alone. The Sequence Number field MUST cycle continuously from 0 to 0xFFFF. The Structure Pointer gives the offset of the first byte of the SONET structure within the packet payload: it locates the J1 byte for SPE emulation and the V5 byte for VT emulation, ranges from 0 to 0xFFE, and MUST be set to 0xFFF if the packet does not carry that byte. The Reserved field MUST be set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

Usage of the RTP header is optional and is a formal reuse of the header format only. RTP mechanisms such as header extensions, the contributing source list, padding, RTCP, header compression and SRTP are not applicable to pseudowires. The Version field MUST be 2, and the padding, extension, CSRC count and marker bits MUST be set to 0 by the sender. The payload type SHOULD come from the dynamic range for each direction of the pseudowire, the sequence number cycles from 0 to 0xFFFF as in RTP, and the timestamp clock MUST be 19.44 MHz based on a local reference. The SSRC field MAY be used to detect misconnections.

For transport over MPLS, the bottom label of the MPLS label stack MUST be used to de-multiplex individual CEP channels. That label is the PW label and the labels above it are tunnel labels. The CEP header follows the generic PWE3 control word format for use over an MPLS packet-switched network.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a CEP header with a few one-bit flags and two counters. One counter numbers the packets so the receiver can spot loss and reordering. The other says where inside the packet the start of the real circuit data sits, because the circuit data does not always begin at the same offset. An RTP header may be added on top for timing, but only the header format is reused, not the rest of RTP.

sections.title: Operation and Packet Synchronization
sections.content:
CEP has two components. The packetizer, or sender, adapts a TDM SONET/SDH signal into a CEP packet stream. The de-packetizer, or receiver, converts the CEP packet stream back into TDM. The de-packetizer needs a jitter buffer to absorb delay variation in the packet stream, and that buffer SHOULD be adjustable in length to account for varying network delay behaviour.

During normal operation the packetizer receives a fixed-rate byte stream from the SONET/SDH interface. When a packet's worth of data has arrived, the necessary headers are prepended to the fragment and the packet is sent into the network. Because all packets for a given channel have the same length, transmission SHOULD occur at regular intervals. At the far end the de-packetizer receives packets into the jitter buffer and plays the byte stream out at a fixed rate onto the SONET/SDH channel.

The CEP sequence numbers detect lost and misordered packets, and the sequence number in the CEP header MUST be used when the RTP header is suppressed. The de-packetizer MUST detect lost or misordered packets, SHOULD play out an all-ones AIS pattern in place of dropped packets, SHOULD re-order packets received out of order, and, if it does not support reordering, MUST drop misordered packets.

Packet synchronization is judged at SONET/SDH play-out time. If the jitter buffer is empty or the packet to be played out has not arrived, the de-packetizer plays out an empty packet made of an all-ones AIS pattern. At startup the de-packetizer is out of packet synchronization by default, and to declare synchronization it must play out a configurable number of CEP packets with sequential sequence numbers. If it then encounters more than a configurable number of sequential empty packets, it MUST declare a Loss of Packet Synchronization (LOPS) defect. LOPS failure is declared after 2.5 +/- 0.5 seconds of LOPS defect and cleared after 10 seconds free of LOPS defect state, and the circuit is considered down for as long as LOPS failure is declared.

Section 10 of the RFC defines counters so an operator can judge the emulated circuit. SONET/SDH defines counters for monitoring service quality, and for CEP to be usable by traditional SONET/SDH network operators it SHOULD provide similar functionality. The near-end monitors are maintained by the de-packetizer during reassembly of the SONET/SDH stream, and they are based on two kinds of defect: type 1, a missing or dropped packet, and type 2, a buffer underrun, a buffer overrun, LOPS, or missing packets above a predefined configurable threshold.

Three counters are defined. ES-CEP counts errored seconds, and each second containing at least one type 1 defect SHALL be declared as ES-CEP. SES-CEP counts severely errored seconds, and each second containing at least one type 2 defect SHALL be declared as SES-CEP. UAS-CEP counts unavailable seconds, and SHALL be declared after a configurable number of consecutive SES-CEP and cleared after a configurable number of consecutive seconds without SES-CEP, with a default value of 10 seconds for each. Once unavailability is declared, ES and SES counts SHALL be inhibited up to the point where the unavailability started; once it is removed, the ES and SES that occurred along the clearing period SHALL be added to the counts. CEP-NE failure is declared after 2.5 +/- 0.5 seconds of CEP-NE type 2 defect and cleared after 10 seconds free of that defect state.

The far-end monitors give insight into the de-packetizer at the far end of the network. They are based on the CEP-RDI indication carried in the R bit: a CEP-FE defect is declared when CEP-RDI is set in the incoming CEP packets. CEP-FE failure is declared after 2.5 +/- 0.5 seconds of CEP-FE defect and cleared after 10 seconds free of CEP-FE defect state.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender cuts the circuit into fixed-size pieces and sends one piece per packet at a steady rate. The receiver puts arriving packets in a buffer and plays them out at the same steady rate onto the optical interface. If a packet does not arrive in time, the receiver plays out a block of ones instead, and after too many such gaps it declares that it has lost synchronization and the circuit is down. Counters record each second in which the circuit carried a loss or a buffer fault.

sections.title: Maintenance Signals and Alarms
sections.content:
SONET/SDH failure indications MUST be transferred correctly over the CEP pseudowire, and CEP connection failures MUST be mapped to SONET/SDH SPE/VT failure indications, so that operators can detect, isolate, monitor and troubleshoot failures the same way they would on a native optical network.

In the SONET/SDH to packet direction, a path outage is signalled with a maintenance alarm such as Path AIS (AIS-P), which means the path is not transmitting valid end-user data and the SPE contains all ones. AIS-V does the same for a Virtual Tributary. During AIS-P/V the CEP packetizer generates packets as usual, MUST set the L bit to 1, and SHOULD set the N and P bits to 1 to indicate loss of pointer. An unequipped indication is used as a trigger for payload removal in the bandwidth-saving modes. The CEP packetizer MUST declare a circuit unequipped only if the Signal Label, Trace (J1/J2) and Tandem Connection (N1/N2/Z6) bytes all have zero value, and during SPE/VT unequipped the N and P bits MUST be interpreted as usual.

In the packet to SONET/SDH direction, the de-packetizer MUST play out one packet's worth of all ones for each CEP packet received with the L bit set, for each packet received during loss of packet synchronization, and for each packet received with both the N and P bits set, which indicates a Loss of Pointer at the far end. In each of those cases it SHOULD also set the pointer value to all ones. A CEP packet whose Length field shows a payload removed by DBA while the L bit is 0 means the removal was triggered by an unequipped indication, and the de-packetizer MUST then transmit a packet of all zeros. The de-packetizer MUST also play out an unequipped indication when the circuit has been de-provisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: A native optical network reports failures with alarm signals, and the emulation has to carry those alarms across the packet network too. The L bit in the CEP header tells the far end that the circuit is broken, and the receiver then plays out a block of ones, which is what an optical network would have shown. The R bit works the other way round, telling the far end that this end has lost synchronization.

sections.title: Pointer Management and Transport Timing
sections.content:
SONET/SDH uses pointers to keep the payload aligned inside the frame. If there is a frequency offset between the frame rate of the transport overhead and that of the SPE, the alignment of the SPE slips back or forward in time through positive or negative stuffing. The same happens between the SPE rate and the rate of a Virtual Tributary it carries. Emulating this aspect of the network can be done in several ways, including Explicit Pointer Adjustment Relay (EPAR) and Adaptive Pointer Management (APM).

Whatever technique is used, the packetizer handles the SPE or VT data the same way. During a negative pointer adjustment event it MUST incorporate the H3 (or V3) byte into the CEP packet payload, and during a positive pointer adjustment event it MUST strip the stuff byte from the payload. When playing out, the de-packetizer MUST place the appropriate byte into the H3 (or V3) position, and MUST insert a stuff byte when playing out a positive adjustment.

EPAR is an optional mechanism that explicitly relays pointer adjustment events across the packet network, and it is only effective when both ends of the pseudowire have access to a common timing reference. Any implementation that does not support EPAR MUST set the N and P bits to 0. The pointer adjustment event MUST be transmitted in three consecutive packets, and the de-packetizer MUST play out the event when any one packet with the N or P bit set is received. The de-packetizer MUST use the CEP sequence numbers so that pointer adjustment events are not played out more often than once per three CEP packets.

For Virtual Tributary emulation, the packetizer relays pointer adjustments received at the SPE level as well as VT-level adjustments, and converts them with an accumulator. A positive adjustment adds a fixed quota and a negative one subtracts it; a VT adjustment changes the accumulator by 783 units, one STS-1 SPE size, while an SPE adjustment changes it by a quota that is a quarter of the VT size, 26 bytes for VT1.5 and 35 bytes for VT2. When the accumulator reaches 783 units a positive adjustment is signalled with the P bit, and when it reaches minus 783 units a negative adjustment is signalled with the N bit. If both N and P are set, a Loss of Pointer event was detected at the ingress and the pointer is invalid, so the de-packetizer MUST play out an AIS-P/V indication.

Transport timing is assumed to come from outside, through Building Integrated Timing Supply, Stand Alone Synchronization Equipment, GPS or a similar mechanism, or from an adaptive timing recovery mechanism. Specific adaptive algorithms are out of scope, but the wander and jitter limits defined in the SDH and SONET standards must be maintained when CEP pseudowires are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical circuits keep their payload aligned with a pointer, and the alignment drifts when the clock rates differ slightly. The RFC describes two ways to handle the drift: relay each adjustment event across the network in the N and P bits, or let the receiver work it out from how full its buffer is. A counter converts the many small adjustments of the fast layer into the fewer, larger adjustments of the slow one.

sections.title: Bandwidth-Saving Options
sections.content:
Beyond pure emulation, CEP offers options that reduce the bandwidth the emulated circuit uses. They fall into two categories. Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (DBA) suppresses transmission of the CEP payload altogether under certain circumstances, such as AIS-P/V and SPE/VT unequipped. Its use depends on the network architecture, for example support of Tandem Connection Monitoring, test signals or Supervisory Unequipped signals. Implementations that support DBA MUST include a way to disable it on a channel-by-channel basis, for interoperability with implementations that do not support it. When a DBA trigger is recognized, the payload is suppressed, the Length field MUST be set to the header lengths alone, and padding bytes SHOULD be added if the intervening network has a minimum packet size larger than the suppressed packet. Apart from the suppression, behaviour is equivalent to normal CEP, and the packet transmission rate during DBA SHOULD be the same as the normal rate.

Service-Specific Payload Formats reduce bandwidth by suppressing parts of the SPE based on specific knowledge of what it carries. Fractional STS-1 (VC-3) encapsulation carries only a selected set of Virtual Tributaries within an STS-1 container. The packetizer removes all fixed column bytes, columns 30 and 59, and all bytes belonging to the removed VTs, keeping only the STS-1 path overhead bytes and the bytes of the selected VTs; the de-packetizer adds the fixed stuff bytes back and generates unequipped VT data in place of the removed VT bytes. An optional bit mask, the Equipped Bit Mask (EBM), says which VTs are carried and which were removed, so a VT can be removed on the fly. Each bit of the 28-bit EBM refers to a different VT, and the 28 bits are divided into seven groups of four, one per Virtual Tributary Group.

The payload size depends on how many tributaries are carried. Each VT1.5 contributes 27 bytes, each VT2 contributes 36 bytes, each VT3 contributes 54 bytes, each VT6 contributes 108 bytes, and the STS-1 path overhead contributes 9 bytes. Asynchronous T3/E3 STS-1 encapsulation may also remove the fixed columns 2, 3, 30, 31, 59 and 60, saving about 7 percent, which gives an actual payload of 729 bytes for a full SPE and 243 bytes for a third-SPE encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tricks reduce the traffic. The first stops sending anything at all while the circuit is broken or idle. The second sends only the parts of the container that carry real traffic and leaves out the empty ones, with a small bit mask telling the far end which ones to rebuild.

sections.title: Signaling of CEP Pseudowires
sections.content:
The CEP pseudowire is set up with the PWE3 control protocol, and the control word is REQUIRED for CEP pseudowires, so the C bit in the PWid FEC and PW generalized ID FEC elements MUST be set. The FEC elements can carry Interface Parameters fields, which validate that the two ends have the capabilities they need to interoperate. Three CEP-specific parameters are defined.

CEP/TDM Payload Bytes MUST contain the expected CEP payload size in bytes, excluding network headers, the CEP header and padding. If payload compression is used, it MUST be set to the uncompressed size as if compression were disabled, so in fractional SPE mode the packet on the wire is normally shorter than advertised. The parameter is OPTIONAL; the default payload size for VT is a single super-frame and for SPE it is 783 bytes. A provider edge that receives a value it does not support locally MUST return the CEP/TDM misconfiguration status error code and the pseudowire MUST NOT be established.

CEP/TDM Bit Rate MUST be set to the data rate in 64-Kbps units of the CEP payload, and again to the uncompressed rate if compression is used. The values are 26 for VT1.5/VC-11, 35 for VT2/VC-12, 53 for VT3, 107 for VT6/VC-2, and 783 times N for STS-Nc with N equal to 1, 3, 12, 48 or 192. The parameter is REQUIRED, and an attempt to establish a pseudowire between peers with different bit rates MUST be rejected with the incompatible bit rate status error code.

CEP Options is also REQUIRED and carries five flags and a type. AIS indicates the sender sends DBA packets when an AIS indication is detected, UNE the same for an unequipped circuit, RTP that packets carry an RTP header, and EBM that packets carry the EBM extension header. The CEP Type field gives 0x0 for SPE mode (STS-1/STS-Mc), 0x1 for VT mode (VT1.5/VT2/VT3/VT6) and 0x2 for fractional SPE (STS-1/VC-3/VC-4). The Async Type field says whether fractional SPE packets use T3 or E3 bandwidth reduction. A provider edge that does not support one of the requested CEP options MUST send a label-release message with the CEP/TDM misconfiguration status code, report it to the operator, and wait for a new consistent label mapping. A pseudowire can be configured asymmetrically, and a provider edge MAY report an asymmetric configuration to the operator.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the pseudowire can carry traffic, both ends must agree on the shape of the circuit. Three parameters do that: how many bytes each packet carries, how fast the circuit runs, and which optional modes each side supports. If the two ends disagree, the setup is rejected rather than left to fail later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The CEP encapsulation is subject to all of the general security considerations discussed in the PWE3 architecture. This document specifies only encapsulations, not the protocols used to carry the encapsulated packets across the packet-switched network, and each such protocol has its own security issues, which are not affected by the encapsulations specified here.

The security of the transported CEP service will only be as good as the security of the packet-switched network, and that may be less rigorous than what a native TDM service offers, because of the inherent differences between circuit-switched and packet-switched public networks. Although CEP MAY employ an RTP header when explicit transfer of timing information is required, the SRTP mechanisms of RFC 3711 are not a substitute for securing the pseudowire and the underlying MPLS network.

The RFC also addresses congestion. CEP pseudowires represent inelastic constant bit rate flows and cannot respond to congestion in a TCP-friendly manner, so they SHOULD be carried across traffic-engineered packet networks that provide bandwidth reservation and admission control, or forwarding prioritization and boundary traffic conditioning. Integrated Services domains supporting Guaranteed Service and Differentiated Services domains supporting Expedited Forwarding are examples of such networks. CEP pseudowires SHOULD monitor packet loss to detect severe congestion, and if severe congestion is detected a CEP pseudowire SHOULD shut down bi-directionally, using the regular pseudowire teardown procedures. The exact criteria for detecting severe congestion and the criteria for restarting afterwards are left for further study. The high availability objectives of the emulated services MUST be taken into account when deciding to shut a pseudowire down temporarily.
sections.plainLanguage: The emulation is only as secure as the packet network that carries it, which may be less secure than a dedicated circuit. Because these circuits run at a fixed rate and cannot slow down when the network is busy, they need a network that reserves capacity for them, and they should be shut down if the network is seriously congested.

WHAT EACH FIELD OF THE CEP HEADER DOES

items.title: L
items.text: Signals CEP-AIS downstream: a failure was detected on the attachment circuit.

items.title: R
items.text: Signals CEP-RDI upstream: this end has lost packet synchronization.

items.title: N and P
items.text: Relay negative and positive pointer adjustments across the packet network. Optional; 0 if unused.

items.title: FRG
items.text: Set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

items.title: Length
items.text: Total length of the CEP header, the RTP header and the payload, or 0 when that exceeds 64 bytes.

items.title: Sequence Number
items.text: Cycles from 0 to 0xFFFF so the receiver can detect lost and misordered packets.

items.title: Structure Pointer
items.text: Offset of the first byte of the SONET structure inside the payload, from 0 to 0xFFE.

items.title: Reserved
items.text: Set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
